                      Precise 3D Robotic Manipulation

Figure 1. Comparison between previous VLA methods and ActiveVLA. Traditional VLA systems often fail in tasks like “bring the
apples on the table” because their fixed cameras miss critical details or become occluded. In contrast, ActiveVLA leverages 3D scene
understanding to freely place virtual cameras and synthesize optimal viewpoints, enabling robots to adjust their view for clearer, more
informative observations and thus achieve more reliable manipulation performance even under occlusion.

Figure 2. The pipeline of ActiveVLA. ActiveVLA is a 3D vision-language-action framework that adopts a two-stage, coarse-to-fine
strategy. In the coarse stage, three orthographic projections of the 3D scene and a language instruction are processed by the PaliGemma
backbone to generate 2D heatmaps, which are then back-projected to locate the most relevant 3D region. In the fine stage, an active
perception module selects new views and performs a 3D zoom-in on this region. The refined PaliGemma then predicts heatmaps for key
end-effector positions, while an action decoder outputs the final 3D action.

RGB, depth, and the coordinates of the points in the world                                                                                                       size H_p \times W_p . Unlike fixed interpolation methods, the up-
frame (3 channels). The coordinates help establish the cor-                                                                                                      sampling module learns pixel-wise weights for finer spatial
respondence of pixels across views, i.e., if pixels from dif-                                                                                                    detail recovery. The pipeline is trained with cross-entropy
ferent views share the same (x, y, z), they correspond to the                                                                                                    loss to predict heatmaps, which are then back-projected
same point in 3D. We use PyTorch3D [51] for rendering.                                                                                                           from all views to identify the crucial 3D region.

                                                                                                                     5. Conclusion
4.2. Ablation Study
                                                                                                                     This paper presents ActiveVLA, a vision-language-action
Component Analysis. We ablate the core active percep-                                                                framework that integrates active perception into robotic ma-
tion modules of ActiveVLA, Active View Selection (A-VS)                                                              nipulation. By incorporating Active View Selection and Ac-
and Active 3D Zoom-in (A-3Z), on an NVIDIA H100 GPU                                                                  tive 3D Zoom-in within a coarse-to-fine architecture, Ac-
across RLBench, COLOSSEUM, and GemBench. The                                                                         tiveVLA enables robots to dynamically adapt their obser-
fixed-view baseline achieves 87.6% success in 0.26 s per                                                             vation strategies for enhanced spatial reasoning and fine-
trial. Adding A-VS dynamically selects informative views,                                                            grained control. By leveraging multi-view 3D perception
raising performance to 89.4% at 0.45 s by improving scene                                                            aligned with VLMs, ActiveVLA effectively balances global
coverage and reducing occlusion. Further introducing A-                                                              context and fine-grained local detail during manipulation.
3Z enables virtual optical zoom for high-resolution close-                                                           Experiments in both simulated and real-world environments
ups, achieving 91.8% success at 0.53 s. These consistent                                                             demonstrate its superior performance across diverse tasks.
